name: Eastern Mnong
sweep_summary: Eastern Mnong (east2333) is not in the catalog. The single sweep item, Simpson 1999 'accents in pop and rock singing' (Multilingua), is a Glottolog keyword-pollution hit ('pop'/'lam') about English singing accents and has no bearing on Mnong; paywalled, no abstract available, priority none. Going beyond the sweep list, I fetched sources the open SEAlang Mon-Khmer Studies holdings on Mnong (Blood 1976 phonemes of Rơlơm; Blood & Blood 1966, 1969; Phillips 1973 x2) to and scanned the two phonological ones. Blood 1976, the first-hand Eastern Mnong (Rơlơm) phonology, is silent on word stress (only a vowel-shortness prosodic feature and an I C (T) syllable pattern). Phillips 1973 mentions 'the main stressed syllable' (p. 120) but is expressly about Central Mnong and excludes Rơlơm. No first-hand Eastern Mnong stress statement was obtained (best_new_statement found=false). Highest-value unreached items for this language: Blood 1963 MA thesis 'The vowel system of Uon Njuñ Mnong Rơlơm' (Indiana), Blood, Blood & Hmok 1976 Mnong Rơlơm dictionary and Hmok 1976 Mnong Lam language lessons (SIL Vietnam; old sil.org repository links dead), and Vietnamese-language grammars/dictionaries (e.g. Nguyễn Kiên Trường & Trương Anh 2009 Từ điển Việt-M'Nông). written in the save directory.

sources.citation: Blood, Henry F. (1976). The phonemes of Uon Njuñ Mnong Rơlơm. Mon-Khmer Studies 5: 4-23.
sources.quote: 5.4 Prosodic Feature. Uon Njuñ Mnong Rơlơm has a shortness feature which occurs as a distinctive feature only with the vowels /i o a u/ and only in closed syllables (syllables having termination). This feature also occurs redundantly on /v/ which is always short (occurring only in closed syllables) and on /o/ in closed syllables. [...] 6.1 Mnong Rơlơm Syllable Pattern. Mnong Rơlơm syllable pattern may be represented by I C (T), in which I (Initiation) and C (Culmination) are obligatory and T (Termination) is optional.
sources.note: First-hand phonology of the Rơlơm dialect (= Eastern Mnong per Glottolog alt. name 'Rolom'), read in full via scanned (no text layer; tesseract 300 dpi). It is SILENT on stress: no occurrence of 'stress', 'accent', 'prominence' or 'presyllable' anywhere in the 20 pages. The only prosodic statement is a vowel-shortness feature (sec. 5.4, p. 15) and the syllable pattern I C (T) (sec. 6.1, p. 16); words are treated at the syllable level only, so no polysyllabic stress rule is given.
